title: Feminines in -α/-η, neuters in -ο/-ι/-μα
goal: Decline the eight noun classes that cover most feminine and neuter nouns.

blocks.text:
Feminines and neuters are simpler than masculines in one way: **nominative = accusative** in each number. Feminines change only in the genitive singular (add -ς) and the plural. Neuters are identical in nominative, accusative and vocative.

What you do have to track is **stress in the genitive plural**. Every genitive plural ends in -ων, and for many classes that ending pulls the stress onto itself: θάλασσα → θαλασσών, τέχνη → τεχνών. Others keep it: ελπίδα → ελπίδων. The table shows which is which.

blocks.title: Feminines in -η
blocks.cite: Holton §3.15, §3.17. The -η/-εις type (πόλη, απόφαση, κυβέρνηση) is the learned ancient third declension; its genitive singular -ης is the everyday form, -εως is formal.

blocks.title: Neuters in -ο and -ι
blocks.cite: Holton §3.22-3.24. -ι neuters add an unstressed ι-glide in gen. sg. and the plural, and that ι is not a syllable: παιδιά [peðʝá].

blocks.title: Neuters in -μα
blocks.cite: Holton §3.26. The stem grows by -ατ- outside the nom./acc. sg., and the stress moves right with it.

blocks.title: Wishes by the calendar
blocks.text: Greek greetings run on the calendar, and they practise every gender. On Mondays people wish each other **Καλή εβδομάδα** 'good week' (feminine), on the first of the month **Καλό μήνα** (masculine), on Fridays **Καλό Σαββατοκύριακο** 'good weekend' (neuter). The big holidays are neuter, several of them plural: **τα Χριστούγεννα** 'Christmas', **τα Θεοφάνεια** 'Epiphany', **το Πάσχα** 'Easter', which never changes form. So you wish **Καλά Χριστούγεννα** with a plural adjective but **Καλό Πάσχα** with a singular one.

**Rule of thumb for the genitive plural.** Almost all feminines in -α and -η move the stress to the ending: ώρα → ωρών, χώρα → χωρών, θάλασσα → θαλασσών, τέχνη → τεχνών. The main exceptions keep it in place: nouns in -ίδα and -άδα (ελπίδα → ελπίδων, εβδομάδα → εβδομάδων) and some learned or foreign words. Neuters in -ο stressed on the third-to-last move it one syllable right (θέατρο → θεάτρων), as do all -μα neuters (αποτελεσμάτων). Drill it rather than memorise lists.

items.why: θάλασσα is stressed on the third-to-last syllable, so -ων pulls the stress onto itself.
Feminines in -ίδα keep the stress: ελπίδων.

items.prompt: Η ιστορία της ___ (η πόλη), everyday Greek
items.why: The everyday genitive of -η/-εις nouns is -ης; -εως is formal; πόλεις is the plural.
-μα neuters add -ατ- and move the stress right: προβλήματα.
Neuter genitive is του; -ι neuters add -ιού.
Neuters in -ο with third-to-last stress shift it one syllable right before -ων.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *the colour of the sea*
items.why: Feminine genitive singular adds -ς: της θάλασσας.
Neuter -ο, third-to-last stress: the stress moves right in the genitive plural.
-μα neuters: genitive singular -ματος, stress moved right.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *the decisions of the government*
items.why: Plural οι αποφάσεις; genitive singular της κυβέρνησης (everyday -ης).
-η/-εις nouns have the genitive plural -εων, with the stress staying put: πόλεων.
The long ending -ου moves the stress: θεάτρου.
